title: Proactive Agents – Kath Korevec, Google Labs

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: The talk's primary focus is Jewels, a proactive asynchronous autonomous coding agent that detects missing tests, unsafe patterns, and suggests code changes within developer repositories. Jewels is a coding assistant product from Google Labs designed to help developers manage async coding tasks in IDE and repository workflows. The talk presents a shipping developer-facing application with current features and planned December enhancements rather than research or infrastructure. The content assumes familiarity with async coding agents and CLI/IDE workflows but is accessible to a broad engineering audience. The video is a conference-style talk by Kath Korevec at the AI Engineer channel. All key claims are directly stated in the transcript with supporting evidence anchors.

summary: Kath Korevec, from Google Labs working on the Ada team, introduces Jewels, a proactive asynchronous autonomous coding agent. She frames the problem with a dishwasher analogy: just as she carried the mental load of reminding her husband to do dishes, developers carry the mental load of monitoring async agents. Humans are serial processors, and context-switching can cost up to 40% of productive time. Current reactive AI tools—waiting for explicit instructions—are insufficient. She envisions dozens of small proactive agents working in parallel, handling tasks like fixing auth bugs, updating configs, and preparing migrations before being asked. She identifies four essential ingredients of proactive systems: observation, personalization, timeliness, and seamless workflow integration. Jewels implements three levels of proactivity. Level one detects and fixes missing tests, unused dependencies, and unsafe patterns during other tasks. Level two observes how developers work and learns frameworks and deployment styles. Level three, shipping in December, converges context with consequence understanding, combining Jewels with Stitch (design agent) and Insights (data agent) for collective intelligence, with humans in the loop. Current features include writable memory, an adversarial critic agent, Playwright verification, a to-do bot, best practices suggestions, an environment agent, and just-in-time context. The walkthrough shows Jewels indexing the ADK Python repository, finding to-dos and best practices with high, medium, and low confidence signals. Users can manually start or delete suggested tasks, drill into code, and see rationale for each suggestion; auto-starting is planned. Kath closes with a Halloween story about building a 6-foot animatronic head, where she used Jules for firmware and LED work but spent most time prompting, waiting, and repeating—unable to focus on creative parts. This gap between tool friction and creative freedom is what Jewels aims to close. She challenges the audience to question old ways of building software, noting that current patterns—IDEs, even code itself—may not exist in six months, and that the future is arriving faster than anyone expects.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and the Mental Load Problem
sections.summary: Kath introduces herself from Google Labs working on the Ada team and the Jewels project. She uses a dishwasher analogy to illustrate mental load: even when not doing the dishes, she tracked whether the task was done. This mirrors how developers babysit async agents today—agents handle work but developers still monitor and follow up.

sections.title: Humans as Serial Processors and the Cost of Context Switching
sections.summary: Humans are serial processors who execute tasks in sequence, not in parallel. Context switching can cost up to 40% of productive time. The viral image of 16 Claude Code tasks on 16 terminals represents an undesirable future DevEx. Developers want collaborators they can trust, not work to manage.

sections.title: From Reactive to Proactive AI Tools
sections.summary: Current AI developer tools are fundamentally reactive, responding only when asked. She envisions a future where compute is not limiting, with dozens of small proactive agents working in parallel—fixing auth bugs, updating configs, flagging errors, preparing migrations—all triggered by natural workflow events.

sections.title: Four Essential Ingredients of Proactive Systems
sections.summary: Proactive systems require observation (continual understanding of code, patterns, workflow), personalization (learning preferences and what to ignore), timeliness (intervening at the right moment), and seamless workflow integration (working in existing terminal, repo, IDE—not a separate application).

sections.title: Familiar Analogies: Nest and the Human Body
sections.summary: Proactivity is not futuristic. Google Nest learns household habits and automates climate control. The human body anticipates falls and elevates heart rate before conscious thought. Proactive AI should feel familiar and human, behaving like a good collaborator rather than a command-line utility.

sections.title: Three Levels of Proactivity in Jewels
sections.summary: Level one: Jewels detects and fixes missing tests, unused dependencies, unsafe patterns during other tasks. Level two: agent observes how you work, learns frameworks and deployment style. Level three: agent understands consequence, converging with Stitch (design) and Insights (data) agents for collective intelligence, with humans firmly in the loop for alignment.

sections.title: Current Jewels Features
sections.summary: Jewels now includes writable memory, an adversarial critic agent for code review, verification via Playwright screenshots, a to-do bot for proactive task pickup, best practices suggestions, an environment agent for setup, and just-in-time context cheat sheets for when the agent gets stuck.

sections.title: Demo Walkthrough: Confidence Signals and Task Management
sections.summary: The walkthrough shows Jewels indexing the ADK Python repository and presenting to-dos and best practices with high, medium, and low confidence signals. Users can manually start or delete tasks, drill into suggested code locations, and view rationale for why the agent wants to work on specific code. Auto-starting tasks is planned for the future.

sections.title: Halloween Animatronic Story: Tool Friction vs Creative Freedom
sections.summary: Kath shares a story about building a 6-foot animatronic head for Halloween with her husband. While he sculpted, she used Jules to update firmware, stepper motors, LEDs, and sensors. She found the prompt-wait-repeat cycle tedious and spent most time fixing bugs and swapping libraries instead of focusing on creative LED animations like eyes following people. She couldn't ship as much as she wanted. This gap between tool friction and creative freedom is what Jewels aims to close.

sections.title: Closing Challenge: Question Old Ways of Building Software
sections.summary: Kath closes by advising that the products built today won't be the products of the future. Current patterns—IDEs, even code itself—may not exist in six to twelve months. She challenges the audience to not be afraid to question old ways of building software, as the future is arriving faster than anyone expects and the people in the room get to build it together.
